name: Adrafinil
lead: Adrafinil is a wakefulness-promoting compound that the body converts to modafinil. People in fitness and self-improvement communities use it to push back against tiredness, which in appearance terms means more energy to train, study and keep routines going, and a less drawn, sleep-deprived look on days when sleep falls short. Grokipedia states it was developed by Laboratoire Lafon in France, marketed there as Olmifon from the mid-1980s for vigilance problems in older adults, and withdrawn in 2011.[1][11]

Because it is a prodrug of modafinil, its central effects are attributed to that metabolite, which acts as a weak inhibitor of the dopamine transporter.[1][2] Adrafinil is not approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for any use and has been sold outside prescription channels in some markets as a supplement or research chemical.[1][11] It is also on doping-control lists as a stimulant, and chemists have published methods to detect it.[3][4]

Published research is mostly early pharmacology, animal behavior studies and case reports. Users on the T Nation forum describe it as a non-prescription alternative to modafinil, with comparisons of how long it lasts and how they feel the next day.[12][13]

paras: In France, adrafinil was authorised in the mid-1980s for vigilance disorders, attention deficits and slowed mental and motor activity in older adults.[1][11] Early use in narcolepsy began in 1977 and 1978 when the sleep researcher Michel Jouvet prescribed it to narcoleptic patients, with inconsistent results.[6] A trial reported on Wikipedia compared adrafinil with clomipramine and placebo in depression and described greater improvement in psychomotor retardation with adrafinil.[11]

subs.h: Use in appearance and fitness communities
paras: Forum users describe adrafinil as a way to get modafinil-like alertness without a prescription.[12][13] A T Nation poster wrote that its effects last about a third as long as modafinil, while another reported that it gave strong concentration and mental stamina but left them tired the next day.[14][15] Other posters describe it as an option when waiting for a modafinil prescription.[16] These accounts are anecdotes; they link adrafinil to appearance only through staying energetic enough to train, study or work.

Two chemists at Laboratoires Lafon identified adrafinil in 1974 while looking for analgesic compounds, and animal tests showed it raised motor activity in mice without peripheral sympathomimetic effects.[6][11] Study of its kinetics led to the identification of its active metabolite, modafinil, in the 1970s, and Jouvet and Bastuji prescribed modafinil to narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia patients in 1983.[6] Modafinil was registered in France in 1992 and later in the US, and was used by the French army in early 1991 during the Gulf War.[6][11]

Adrafinil reached the French market in 1984 or 1985 as Olmifon. Lafon was acquired by Cephalon in 2001, and Olmifon was discontinued in September 2011 with the manufacturer citing an unfavorable risk-benefit ratio compared with modafinil, which stayed on the market.[11]

Adrafinil and modafinil come from the same benzhydryl sulfinyl series developed in France in the 1970s by the neurophysiologist Michel Jouvet and Lafon Laboratories; modafinil is adrafinil's primary active metabolite.[26] France approved modafinil in 1994 as Modiodal, the US FDA approved it in 1998 for narcolepsy as Provigil, and it later gained indications for shift work sleep disorder and sleepiness from obstructive sleep apnea in 2003.[26] The UK approved it in December 2002, armodafinil arrived in 2007, and generic modafinil became available in the US in 2012.[26]

Modafinil is described as an atypical dopamine reuptake inhibitor whose exact mechanism is not fully understood, with indirect effects on norepinephrine, serotonin, orexin, histamine, glutamate and GABA.[26] Among healthy people it is used as a so-called smart drug by students and office workers. Reported effects range from significant cognitive improvement to little or none, benefits appear more noticeable in sleep-deprived people, and experts caution that although modafinil has low abuse potential it acts on some of the same mechanisms as addictive stimulants.[26] Modafinil is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US, prescription-only in the UK, a Schedule II controlled substance in Russia since 2012, and has been banned by WADA since 3 August 2004.[26]

Adrafinil has little direct activity before metabolism. The liver converts it to modafinil, which is a weak, atypical dopamine transporter blocker; modulation of orexin, histamine, glutamate and other systems has also been proposed, and the full mechanism is not settled.[1][2] An early idea that adrafinil acted as an alpha-1 adrenergic agonist has been described as lacking support from binding studies.[1][11]

Wikipedia describes adrafinil as having an elimination half-life of about one hour, compared with 12 to 15 hours for modafinil, with effects on an empty stomach starting around 45 to 60 minutes after an oral dose.[1][11] Modafinil itself is metabolized mainly in the liver to inactive acid and sulfone metabolites that are excreted by the kidneys.[2] A 2008 study reported the pharmacokinetics of adrafinil in rats.[17]

Reported effects of adrafinil include stomach pain, skin irritation, anxiety and, with prolonged use, raised liver enzymes.[11] A case report described orofacial dyskinesia, abnormal mouth and face movements, in a patient taking adrafinil that did not resolve for four months after withdrawal and later improved with tetrabenazine.[18] Modafinil's reported effects include headache, insomnia, anxiety, diarrhea, dry mouth and raised blood pressure and heart rate.[2] Reviewers have noted that modafinil's unsupervised use raises questions about health problems that are not fully understood.[2]

Adrafinil is a diarylmethane sulfoxide hydroxamic acid, the N-hydroxylated analogue of modafinil, with formula C15H15NO3S.[11] Analytical papers have separated adrafinil from modafinil enantiomers by chromatography and developed fluorescent sensors to detect it, and a 2017 study examined how modafinil, adrafinil and related compounds break down in gas chromatography injectors.[4][5][19] A 2025 paper described validated methods for identifying novel modafinil analogs in products sold as dietary supplements.[20]

Adrafinil has never been approved by the FDA, and Wikipedia reports that the agency treats its use in supplements as unlawful, citing a rejected 2017 new dietary ingredient notification, a 2019 warning letter and later enforcement actions.[1][11] It is listed as Schedule 4 prescription-only in Australia.[11] Adrafinil and modafinil were added to the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list in 2004, and reviews of stimulants in sport discuss them alongside caffeine, ephedrines and amphetamines.[3][11]

Threads on T Nation mention adrafinil within broader nootropic and productivity discussions, often alongside modafinil, caffeine and other stimulants.[12][21] Some posters describe it as a 'weaker' option that smoothed out highs and lows, while others report next-day fatigue.[15][22]

No studies of adrafinil for appearance outcomes were found. Human clinical research on adrafinil is limited and mostly runs through the modafinil metabolite.[1] A review of eugeroics in affective disorders groups adrafinil with modafinil and armodafinil and reports that most evidence is for modafinil.[23]

Animal research includes behavioral studies in aged dogs. In a randomized comparison of 36 beagles aged 9 to 16 years given adrafinil, propentofylline or nicergoline for 33 days, only adrafinil increased locomotion in open-field tests, and the authors concluded it may improve exploratory behavior and alertness in aged dogs.[8] Other studies in aged canines examined behavior and discrimination learning, and the canine ageing model has been used to evaluate cognition-enhancing drugs.[7][9][24][25] In mice, adrafinil was one of several stimulants used to test how increased locomotion affects indices of anxiety in a light/dark box.[10]

lore.intro: On forums such as T Nation, adrafinil appears in nootropic and productivity threads as a non-prescription route to modafinil-like effects.[12][21]

claims.claim: Adrafinil gives the same alertness as modafinil without a prescription
claims.believers: Posters say it 'does the exact same thing' as modafinil and does not need a prescription, though its effects are shorter and it is 'not as safe to use'.[14][16]
claims.experts: Adrafinil is a prodrug converted to modafinil, so effects are attributed to that metabolite; adrafinil's half-life is about one hour versus 12 to 15 hours for modafinil, and it has been linked to raised liver enzymes with prolonged use.[1][11]

claims.believers: One poster said it 'smoothed out the highs and lows' compared with modafinil.[22]
claims.experts: No published human trial has compared the subjective smoothness of adrafinil and modafinil.

claims.claim: Adrafinil boosts concentration but costs energy the next day
claims.believers: A poster found it fantastic for concentration and mental stamina but said it wiped them out the next day.[15]
claims.experts: No controlled human trials of next-day effects are available; modafinil's reported effects include insomnia and anxiety.[2]

card.summary: A modafinil prodrug once sold in France; no appearance use has been studied and human data are thin.
card.note: Not FDA-approved; withdrawn from the French market in 2011 per Grokipedia.

quick.overview:
Adrafinil is converted by the liver into modafinil. It was sold in France as Olmifon for sleepiness and inattention in older adults until 2011 and is not approved in the US.
No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes, and little human clinical research exists.
quick.mechanism: It is a prodrug: the liver metabolises it to modafinil, which acts on the dopamine transporter.
quick.risks: Human safety data are limited. It is listed as a stimulant in doping control and is not approved for any use in the US.

chain: Converted by the liver to modafinil
More energy for workouts, study and routines on low-sleep days
angle.text: People who use adrafinil describe it as a way to stay alert and keep training or working when tired. The link to appearance runs through energy and consistency: more sessions completed and a less fatigued look, rather than any direct effect on skin, hair or body composition.
